mcq.q: 7 items are chosen; each is defective with probability 1/3. Find the chance that exactly 2 of them are defective.
mcq.explain: Binomial: P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ with n = 7, p = 1/3, q = 2/3, r = 2. So P = 7C2 × (1/3)^2 × (2/3)^5 = 21 × 1/9 × 32/243 = 224/729. Forgetting ⁿCᵣ counts only one order of successes.
mcq.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcq.fast: ⁿCᵣ × pʳ × qⁿ⁻ʳ — compute the numerator and the denominator separately.

mcq.q: A student guesses 4 questions, each correct with probability 1/2. Find the chance that exactly 1 of them is correct.
mcq.explain: Binomial: P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ with n = 4, p = 1/2, q = 1/2, r = 1. So P = 4C1 × (1/2)^1 × (1/2)^3 = 4 × 1/2 × 1/8 = 1/4. Forgetting ⁿCᵣ counts only one order of successes.
mcq.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcq.fast: ⁿCᵣ × pʳ × qⁿ⁻ʳ — compute the numerator and the denominator separately.

mcq.q: 3 items are chosen; each is defective with probability 2/5. Find the chance that exactly 2 of them are defective.
mcq.explain: Binomial: P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ with n = 3, p = 2/5, q = 3/5, r = 2. So P = 3C2 × (2/5)^2 × (3/5)^1 = 3 × 4/25 × 3/5 = 36/125. Forgetting ⁿCᵣ counts only one order of successes.
mcq.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcq.fast: ⁿCᵣ × pʳ × qⁿ⁻ʳ — compute the numerator and the denominator separately.

mcq.q: The probability that a machine part is defective is 1/4. In a sample of 3 parts, the probability of at least one defective is:
mcq.explain: "At least one" is the complement of "none": P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − q^n = 1 − (3/4)^3 = 1 − 27/64 = 37/64. Adding P(X = 1), P(X = 2), … one by one is much slower and error-prone.
mcq.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcq.fast: At least one = 1 − qⁿ (complement of none).

mcq.q: The probability that a machine part is defective is 1/5. In a sample of 6 parts, the probability of at least one defective is:
mcq.explain: "At least one" is the complement of "none": P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − q^n = 1 − (4/5)^6 = 1 − 4096/15625 = 11529/15625. Adding P(X = 1), P(X = 2), … one by one is much slower and error-prone.
mcq.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcq.fast: At least one = 1 − qⁿ (complement of none).

mcq.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 91 and p = 0.4, the variance is:
mcq.explain: Binomial mean = np = 91 × 0.4 = 36.4; variance = npq = 91 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 21.84; SD = √(npq). So the variance is 21.84. The variance of a binomial is always smaller than its mean because q < 1.
mcq.fast: Mean np, variance npq, SD √(npq).

mcq.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 17 and p = 0.6, the mean is:
mcq.explain: Binomial mean = np = 17 × 0.6 = 10.2; variance = npq = 17 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 4.08; SD = √(npq). So the mean is 10.2. The variance of a binomial is always smaller than its mean because q < 1.
mcq.fast: Mean np, variance npq, SD √(npq).

mcq.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 48 and p = 0.2, the variance is:
mcq.explain: Binomial mean = np = 48 × 0.2 = 9.6; variance = npq = 48 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 7.68; SD = √(npq). So the variance is 7.68. The variance of a binomial is always smaller than its mean because q < 1.
mcq.fast: Mean np, variance npq, SD √(npq).

mcq.q: A binomial distribution has mean 8.4 and variance 6.72. The value of p is:
mcq.explain: Variance ÷ mean = npq/np = q, so q = 6.72/8.4 = 0.8 and p = 1 − q = 0.2. Then n = mean/p = 8.4/0.2 = 42. Taking q as p is the usual error.
mcq.fast: q = variance ÷ mean; p = 1 − q; n = mean ÷ p.

mcq.q: A binomial distribution has mean 18.4 and variance 11.04. The value of n is:
mcq.explain: Variance ÷ mean = npq/np = q, so q = 11.04/18.4 = 0.6 and p = 1 − q = 0.4. Then n = mean/p = 18.4/0.4 = 46. Taking q as p is the usual error.
mcq.fast: q = variance ÷ mean; p = 1 − q; n = mean ÷ p.

mcq.q: The number of printing mistakes per page of a book follows a Poisson distribution with mean 0.5. Given e^(−0.5) = 0.6065, the probability of exactly 0 is about:
mcq.explain: Poisson: P(X = r) = e^(−m) mʳ/r!. With m = 0.5 and r = 0: 0.6065 × 0.5^0/0! = 0.6065 × 1/1 = 0.6065. Forgetting to divide by r! gives too large a value. In a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both equal to m.
mcq.fast: e^(−m) × mʳ ÷ r! — use the e^(−m) value given in the question.

mcq.q: The number of defects per metre of cloth follows a Poisson distribution with mean 4. Given e^(−4) = 0.0183, the probability of exactly 4 is about:
mcq.explain: Poisson: P(X = r) = e^(−m) mʳ/r!. With m = 4 and r = 4: 0.0183 × 4^4/4! = 0.0183 × 256/24 = 0.1952. Forgetting to divide by r! gives too large a value. In a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both equal to m.
mcq.fast: e^(−m) × mʳ ÷ r! — use the e^(−m) value given in the question.

mcq.q: The number of defects per metre of cloth follows a Poisson distribution with mean 1. Given e^(−1) = 0.3679, the probability of exactly 4 is about:
mcq.explain: Poisson: P(X = r) = e^(−m) mʳ/r!. With m = 1 and r = 4: 0.3679 × 1^4/4! = 0.3679 × 1/24 = 0.0153. Forgetting to divide by r! gives too large a value. In a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both equal to m.
mcq.fast: e^(−m) × mʳ ÷ r! — use the e^(−m) value given in the question.

mcq.q: For a Poisson variate X, P(X = 3) = P(X = 4). The mean of the distribution is:
mcq.explain: e^(−m)m^3/3! = e^(−m)m^4/4!. Cancel e^(−m) m^3/3!: 1 = m/4, so m = 4. In general P(X = r) = P(X = r + 1) gives m = r + 1. The mean of a Poisson distribution equals its variance.

mcq.q: For a Poisson variate X, P(X = 4) = P(X = 5). The standard deviation of X is:
mcq.explain: P(X = 4) = P(X = 5) gives m = 5 = 5. For a Poisson distribution, mean = variance = m, so SD = √m = √5 ≈ 2.2361. Giving the variance (5) as the SD is the trap.
mcq.fast: m = r + 1; SD = √m.

mcq.q: The probability that an item is defective is 1/1000. Using the Poisson approximation (e^(−2) = 0.1353), the probability that a box of 2000 items contains no defective is about:
mcq.explain: n is large and p is small, so use Poisson with m = np = 2000 × 1/1000 = 2. P(X = 0) = e^(−2) × 2^0/0! = 0.1353. Poisson suits rare events: many trials, each with a tiny chance.
mcq.fast: m = np, then e^(−m) mʳ/r!.

mcq.q: The probability that an item is defective is 1/100. Using the Poisson approximation (e^(−5) = 0.0067), the probability that a box of 500 items contains no defective is about:
mcq.explain: n is large and p is small, so use Poisson with m = np = 500 × 1/100 = 5. P(X = 0) = e^(−5) × 5^0/0! = 0.0067. Poisson suits rare events: many trials, each with a tiny chance.
mcq.fast: m = np, then e^(−m) mʳ/r!.

mcq.q: X is normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 2. The standard normal variate z for x = 66 is:
mcq.explain: z = (x − μ)/σ = (66 − 70)/2 = -2. z measures how many standard deviations x lies from the mean; a negative z means x is below the mean. Dividing by the variance instead of the SD is a common slip.
mcq.topic: Standard normal variate and using the table
mcq.fast: Subtract the mean, divide by the SD.

mcq.q: X is normally distributed with mean 166 and standard deviation 22. The standard normal variate z for x = 210 is:
mcq.explain: z = (x − μ)/σ = (210 − 166)/22 = 2. z measures how many standard deviations x lies from the mean; a negative z means x is below the mean. Dividing by the variance instead of the SD is a common slip.
mcq.topic: Standard normal variate and using the table
mcq.fast: Subtract the mean, divide by the SD.

mcq.q: X is normal with mean 117 and SD 20. Given that the area under the standard normal curve between z = 0 and z = 0.5 is 0.1915, the probability that X is more than 127 is:
mcq.explain: Convert to z: z = (x − 117)/20. The normal curve is symmetric and each half has area 0.5. P(X > 127) = 0.5 − (area 0 to 0.5) = 0.5 − 0.1915 = 0.3085. Draw the curve and shade the region before adding or subtracting.
mcq.fast: Sketch the bell, shade, then add areas on opposite sides of the mean or subtract on the same side.

mcq.q: X is normal with mean 134 and SD 4. Given that the areas between z = 0 and z = 2 and between z = 0 and z = 1.25 are 0.4772 and 0.3944, the probability that X is between 126 and 139 is:
mcq.explain: Convert to z: z = (x − 134)/4. The normal curve is symmetric and each half has area 0.5. The interval crosses the mean, so add the two areas: 0.8716. Draw the curve and shade the region before adding or subtracting.
mcq.fast: Sketch the bell, shade, then add areas on opposite sides of the mean or subtract on the same side.

mcq.q: X is normal with mean 50 and SD 12. Given that the area between z = 0 and z = 1.25 is 0.3944, the probability that X is less than 65 is:
mcq.explain: Convert to z: z = (x − 50)/12. The normal curve is symmetric and each half has area 0.5. P(X < 65) = 0.5 + 0.3944 = 0.8944. Draw the curve and shade the region before adding or subtracting.
mcq.fast: Sketch the bell, shade, then add areas on opposite sides of the mean or subtract on the same side.

mcq.q: X is normal with mean 145 and SD 4. Given that the area under the standard normal curve between z = 0 and z = 2 is 0.4772, the probability that X is more than 153 is:
mcq.explain: Convert to z: z = (x − 145)/4. The normal curve is symmetric and each half has area 0.5. P(X > 153) = 0.5 − (area 0 to 2) = 0.5 − 0.4772 = 0.0228. Draw the curve and shade the region before adding or subtracting.
mcq.fast: Sketch the bell, shade, then add areas on opposite sides of the mean or subtract on the same side.

mcq.q: Marks of 500 students are normally distributed with mean 63 and SD 10. Given that the area between z = 0 and z = 2 is 0.4772, about how many students score above 83?
mcq.explain: z = (83 − 63)/10 = 2. P(X > 83) = 0.5 − 0.4772 = 0.0228. Expected number = 500 × 0.0228 ≈ 11. Multiplying N by the table area itself counts students between the mean and 83.
mcq.fast: Tail area = 0.5 − table area; multiply by the number of students.

mcq.q: Marks of 2,000 students are normally distributed with mean 44 and SD 8. Given that the area between z = 0 and z = 1 is 0.3413, about how many students score above 52?
mcq.explain: z = (52 − 44)/8 = 1. P(X > 52) = 0.5 − 0.3413 = 0.1587. Expected number = 2,000 × 0.1587 ≈ 317. Multiplying N by the table area itself counts students between the mean and 52.
mcq.fast: Tail area = 0.5 − table area; multiply by the number of students.

mcq.q: For a normal distribution the mean deviation about the mean is 28. The standard deviation is approximately:
mcq.explain: For a normal distribution, MD ≈ (4/5)σ, so σ ≈ (5/4) × MD = 1.25 × 28 = 35. Multiplying by 4/5 again goes the wrong way. The SD is always larger than the mean deviation for a normal curve.
mcq.fast: For a normal curve σ ≈ 1.25 × mean deviation.

mcq.q: For a normal distribution the mean deviation about the mean is 12. The standard deviation is approximately:
mcq.explain: For a normal distribution, MD ≈ (4/5)σ, so σ ≈ (5/4) × MD = 1.25 × 12 = 15. Multiplying by 4/5 again goes the wrong way. The SD is always larger than the mean deviation for a normal curve.
mcq.fast: For a normal curve σ ≈ 1.25 × mean deviation.
